questions.question: Why does an indefinite integral always carry +C, and why does a DEFINITE integral not need it?
questions.solution: Differentiation destroys constants, so an antiderivative is only determined up to an arbitrary constant — the family of curves y = F(x) + C. In a definite integral the constant cancels: [F(b)+C] − [F(a)+C] = F(b) − F(a). Omitting +C in indefinite work is an error; carrying it into definite work is just noise.

questions.question: Compute ∫₀³ |x − 1| dx conceptually — why does a single antiderivative evaluation fail here?
questions.solution: The integrand changes form at x = 1 (where x−1 = 0), so it must be SPLIT: ∫₀¹ (1−x) dx + ∫₁³ (x−1) dx = ½ + 2 = 2.5. A single antiderivative of |x−1| is not differentiable at 1; the fundamental theorem needs a smooth integrand on the whole interval. Signed area means the negative lobe counts as negative — splitting is the standard technique.

questions.concept: Integration by parts — choosing u and dv
questions.question: For ∫ x·eˣ dx, why choose u = x and dv = eˣ dx rather than the reverse? State the selection heuristic.
questions.solution: By parts: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. The goal is that ∫v du is EASIER than the original. With u = x, du = dx and ∫eˣ dx is trivial — the polynomial power drops. Reversed, u = eˣ gives ∫x·eˣ dx again — no progress. Heuristic (ILATE): pick u as Inverse, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential in that priority order.

questions.question: Why does ∫2x·cos(x²) dx become simply sin(x²) + C? Identify the 'inside function' the substitution targets.
questions.solution: The integrand contains a function and its derivative as a factor: d/dx(x²) = 2x. Substituting u = x², du = 2x dx reduces it to ∫cos u du = sin u + C. Substitution reverses the CHAIN rule — spot the composite (x²) and its derivative multiplier, and the integral collapses.

questions.question: Evaluate ∫₋₂² x³ dx without any antiderivative, and state the general property used.
questions.solution: x³ is ODD: f(−x) = −f(x), so the negative-area lobe exactly cancels the positive one over a symmetric interval — the integral is 0. Property: ∫₋ₐₐ f = 0 for odd f, and = 2∫₀ₐ f for even f. Recognising parity saves the whole computation; checking parity FIRST is the examinable habit.

questions.question: Why can ∫dx/(x²−1) be split into two simple logs, while ∫dx/(x²+1) cannot?
questions.solution: x²−1 factors over the reals into (x−1)(x+1), so 1/(x²−1) = ½[1/(x−1) − 1/(x+1)] → ½ln|(x−1)/(x+1)| + C. x²+1 has no real linear factors — it is irreducible over ℝ, giving arctan x + C instead. Partial fractions need REAL LINEAR factors; irreducible quadratics go to arctan.

questions.question: Explain why ∫ₐᵇ f = −∫ᵦₐ f, and use the property to evaluate ∫₃¹ (2x) dx given ∫₁³ (2x) dx = 8.
questions.solution: Swapping the limits reverses the direction of accumulation: each infinitesimal strip dxF is now subtracted instead of added, negating the total. So ∫₃¹ (2x) dx = −8. The property is the algebraic backbone of interval-splitting: ∫ₐᶜ = ∫ₐᵇ + ∫ᵦ꜀ requires consistent direction.

questions.concept: Area between curves — subtract in the right order
questions.question: Find the area between y = x and y = x² from x = 0 to 1, and explain why naive subtraction of antiderivatives can give a negative area.
questions.solution: On (0,1), x ≥ x², so A = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = ½ − ⅓ = 1/6. If you subtract in the wrong order (x² − x) the integral is −1/6: the SIGN records which curve was on top. Take |top − bottom| per interval — identify the upper curve first, then integrate the difference.
